At £10,000 of earnings, qualifying earnings are £3,760. At 5%, the employee contribution is £188 and the employer contributes £112.80. Automatic enrolment does not normally apply the minimum percentage to every pound of salary. GOV.UK describes most automatic-enrolment schemes as basing contributions on total earnings between £6,240 and £50,270 a year before tax. Those are the band limits used here. Earnings below the lower limit produce no qualifying earnings in this simplified model. Earnings above the upper limit do not increase the contribution base.

Automatic-enrolment contributions apply to earnings between two limits, not to the whole salary. The employee’s gross contribution can be the same under net pay and relief at source, while the take-home cost differs when there is little or no Income Tax to relieve.

Below HK$7,100, no employee mandatory contribution is required, while the employer still contributes 5% of relevant income. From HK$7,100 through HK$30,000, the employee and employer each contribute 5%. Above HK$30,000, each mandatory amount is capped at HK$1,500.

The employee amount is deducted from relevant income. The employer amount is funded separately by the employer. Deducting both amounts from the employee’s HK$20,000 would count the employer obligation against the wrong cash source.

The employee deduction affects the income left after MPF. The employer pays a separate mandatory amount from its own funds. Both calculations depend on the relevant-income rules and the applicable boundaries.

The employer amount is also not free money in the sense of being available for other spending. It is paid by the employer into the pension instead of being paid as salary in this comparison. The model does not assume that rejecting the pension would raise salary by the same amount.

The employer’s own contribution is not deducted from the employee’s income a second time. The endpoint is not a verified bank deposit, final take-home pay or disposable income: tax, other deductions, income classification and actual payment timing remain outside the model. The employee contribution is transferred toward retirement provision, rather than treated as money destroyed.

The first step is the amount taken from take-home pay. The basic-rate top-up is 20% of the gross contribution, or 25% of the net payment. When higher-rate tax applies, the provider still adds only the basic 20%. Any additional higher-rate relief is claimed from HMRC and paid to the employee rather than added to the pension pot, so it is deliberately outside this bridge. The endpoint is the gross contribution credited before any investment movement or fee, not a cash amount available to spend. Scottish relief-at-source rules can differ, and the source notes that a 19% Scottish rate still receives a 20% at-source claim.

The fixed scenarios show the lower boundary and the cap without connecting a false continuous line across the employee threshold. At HK$7,099 the employee amount is zero; at HK$7,100 it is HK$355. The employer does not have that minimum-income exemption. These are calculated examples, not observed wages or contribution records.

The fixed scenarios use the selected rates but replace annual earnings. A salary below £6,240 produces no qualifying earnings in this simplified band model; eligibility or a right to join must be checked separately. Between the limits, £1 more of earnings adds the selected percentage to each side. Above £50,270 the contribution amounts stay flat because only £44,030 of earnings is inside the band. The bars are calculated contributions, not observed payroll deductions.

The flat contribution above the upper limit is also an arithmetic result of the band, not a cap on what an employer or employee may contribute. Additional voluntary contributions, salary sacrifice and scheme-specific rates are outside the model.

The grouped chart shows full monthly scenarios around those boundaries. It does not infer an employee’s eligibility or apply these monthly thresholds to a weekly, daily, partial-month or casual-worker calculation.

The legal minimum from April 2019 is 3% from the employer and 5% from the employee, for 8% in total. Scheme rules can require more, and a scheme may use a different definition of pensionable pay. The model therefore applies the selected rates to the band, not to gross salary, and states that choice rather than presenting it as every workplace scheme.

The model does not calculate salary sacrifice. Under salary sacrifice, the employee gives up salary in exchange for an employer pension contribution, which can change National Insurance and the contractual pay figure. It is a different arrangement from either net pay or relief at source and is not treated as equivalent here.

The pay-record and remittance information also distinguishes the relevant income, employee and employer contributions, and payment date. Those records help reconcile the payroll deduction with money later credited under the applicable arrangements.

The rule still applies 5% to a maximum HK$30,000 income base. It does not apply 5% to every dollar above that level. The percentage curve begins at HK$7,100, where employee contributions apply, and retains the separate 5% comparison.
